title: Human Spleen Anatomy: Red Pulp, White Pulp & Blood Flow
description: Explore human spleen anatomy in the left upper abdomen, including the fibrous capsule, splenic hilum, immune white pulp follicles, and red pulp filtration.
h1: Human Spleen Anatomy: Red Pulp, White Pulp, Hilum and Vessels
blurb: Tucked beneath the left ribs, the spleen pairs immune white-pulp lymphoid follicles with filtering red-pulp cords that recycle aging red blood cells.
lead: Protected beneath ribs nine through eleven in the upper left abdomen, the spleen is the largest lymphoid organ in the body and a precision filter for circulating blood. In this illustrated guide to human spleen anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including capsule & trabeculae, red pulp, white pulp, splenic sinusoids—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Protected beneath ribs nine through eleven in the upper left abdomen, the spleen is the largest lymphoid organ in the body and a precision filter for circulating blood. Blood enters the spleen through the splenic artery and percolates through two compartments. White pulp — cuffs of lymphocytes around central arterioles — mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens, making IgM and opsonins. Red pulp is a mesh of sinusoids and cords where old, stiff or antibody-coated red cells are trapped and destroyed by macrophages, and where platelets are stored (a third of the body's pool). In fetal life the spleen makes red cells; after splenectomy the liver and marrow take over, but the loss of opsonisation leaves lifelong risk of encapsulated bacterial sepsis. Within the human body, the spleen (Lien (splen)) is situated in left hypochondrium, ribs 9–11, posterior to the stomach, receives arterial perfusion via splenic artery (largest branch of the coeliac trunk), and is innervated by coeliac plexus (sympathetic) — mostly vasomotor.

The capsule & trabeculae (Capsula lienis) is a fibroelastic capsule sending trabeculae into the pulp, carrying the vessels. Physiologically, the capsule & trabeculae governs structural framework and conduit for vessels. Structurally, the red pulp (Pulpa rubra) comprises splenic cords of Billroth and wide sinusoids lined by stave cells with slit-like gaps. Physiologically, the red pulp filters senescent and abnormal red cells; recycles iron; stores platelets and monocytes. Structurally, the white pulp (Pulpa alba) comprises periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (T cells), follicles (B cells) and a marginal zone rich in macrophages. Physiologically, the white pulp governs immune surveillance of blood: antibody and opsonin production, especially against capsules. Structurally, the splenic sinusoids (Sinus splenicus) comprises discontinuous, leaky channels whose endothelial slits force red cells to squeeze through. Physiologically, the splenic sinusoids governs the mechanical filter: healthy deformable cells pass; rigid ones are eaten. The hilum (Hilum lienis) is the notched medial border where splenic vessels enter and the tail of pancreas and stomach fundus relate. Physiologically, the hilum governs vascular gateway; also the site of accessory spleens in ~15% of people. The splenic artery (Arteria lienalis) is a tortuous branch of the coeliac trunk running along the upper border of the pancreas. Physiologically, the splenic artery supplies the spleen, pancreas (via branches) and part of the stomach.

Clinically, regarding the capsule & trabeculae, the capsule is thin and the pulp fragile — the spleen tears easily in blunt abdominal trauma and bleeds briskly. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the red pulp, in hereditary spherocytosis the rigid spheres are trapped here, causing haemolytic anaemia cured by splenectomy. In clinical pathology involving the white pulp, its loss explains why asplenic patients are vulnerable to pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae. Medical evaluation of the splenic sinusoids also notes that malaria parasites stiffen red cells, which is why the spleen enlarges in chronic infection.

questions.question: What is the spleen's function?
questions.answer: The spleen filters blood, removes aging red blood cells and helps immune cells respond to blood-borne material. Its red and white pulp perform different tasks.

questions.question: Can you feel a normal spleen?
questions.answer: A normal adult spleen is usually protected beneath the left lower ribs and is not readily felt on examination; enlargement is a medical finding, not something this atlas can diagnose.

questions.question: What are the splenic capsule and trabeculae?
questions.answer: The spleen’s fibroelastic capsule sends trabeculae into the pulp; these trabeculae carry blood vessels.

questions.question: Where is the white pulp located?
questions.answer: White pulp is within the spleen, surrounding central arterioles as periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths and follicles.

questions.question: What structures pass through the splenic hilum?
questions.answer: The splenic artery and vein, lymphatics and nerves pass through the hilum; the pancreatic tail lies nearby.
